title: The Marathas
description: An illustrated map of the Marathas, from the saint-poets of Pandharpur and Shivaji’s hill forts through the war with Aurangzeb, the Peshwas’ armies reaching Delhi, Bengal and Attock, the disaster at Panipat and the great Maratha houses, to the British victory in 1818 and the forts listed by UNESCO in 2025.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the Maratha kingdom and confederacy, from 1630 to 1818
note: Based on Maratha chronicles (bakhars) and letters, Mughal and Persian histories, Portuguese, English and Dutch records, and later historians. Some episodes are known mainly from tradition and are labelled so in the text. Army sizes and death tolls are disputed estimates. The map is stylised and not to scale; the areas under Powers are painted loosely and are not borders.

steps.title: Saints of the Deccan
steps.text: Long before any Maratha kingdom, Marathi had a literature of its own. Tradition dates the saint-poet Dnyaneshwar’s Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita to 1290; Eknath and Tukaram followed. Their followers, the Varkaris, walk each year to the god Vithoba at Pandharpur. Many historians see this shared devotion in Marathi as one root of Maratha identity.
steps.today: Today: Pandharpur, Maharashtra, where huge crowds still arrive each year on the wari pilgrimage.

steps.title: Born at Shivneri
steps.text: Shahaji Bhosale, a Maratha commander, served the sultans of Ahmadnagar and then Bijapur, who granted him lands around Pune. His son Shivaji was born in the hill fort of Shivneri. The Maharashtra government marks 19 February 1630; some traditions give 1627. Shahaji served Bijapur mostly in the south, and Shivaji grew up with his mother, Jijabai.
steps.today: Today: Shivneri fort, above Junnar, Pune district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Forts above Pune
steps.text: Jijabai and the young Shivaji settled at Pune, on Shahaji’s lands, run by the administrator Dadoji Konddev. In his teens Shivaji began taking hill forts held loosely for Bijapur. Torna came first, by tradition in 1646; he built Rajgad nearby as his capital. In 1656 he seized Javali from the More family, opening the road to the Konkan coast.
steps.today: Today: Pune, Maharashtra; Torna and Rajgad lie to its south-west.

steps.title: Afzal Khan at Pratapgad
steps.text: Bijapur sent its general Afzal Khan with a large army to crush Shivaji. Shivaji stayed in the forest fort of Pratapgad and agreed to meet him alone below its walls. At the meeting Afzal Khan was killed; Maratha accounts say he struck first and Shivaji, wearing tiger claws (wagh nakh), struck back. The leaderless Bijapur army was then routed.
steps.today: Today: Pratapgad, near Mahabaleshwar, Maharashtra, with Afzal Khan’s tomb below the fort.

steps.title: The pass at Pavan Khind
steps.text: Siddi Jauhar’s Bijapur army besieged Shivaji in Panhala for months. On a rainy July night he slipped out towards Vishalgad, some 60 kilometres away. Baji Prabhu Deshpande held a narrow pass behind him with a few hundred men until guns from Vishalgad signalled Shivaji’s arrival. Baji Prabhu died there; the pass was renamed Pavan Khind, the sacred pass.
steps.today: Today: Panhala, Kolhapur district; trekkers walk the night route to Pavan Khind each year.

steps.title: A night raid on the Lal Mahal
steps.text: Aurangzeb sent his uncle Shaista Khan against Shivaji. He took Pune and lived in the Lal Mahal, Shivaji’s own childhood house. One night in April 1663 Shivaji and a small band slipped into the town, by tradition among a wedding party, and broke into the house. Shaista Khan escaped with the loss of fingers and was soon recalled.
steps.today: Today: a rebuilt Lal Mahal in Pune’s old city, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The sack of Surat
steps.text: Surat was the Mughal empire’s richest port, where pilgrims sailed for Mecca and the English and Dutch kept trading houses. In January 1664 Shivaji’s cavalry raided the town for several days and carried off a great treasure. The English and Dutch defended their warehouses, and the Mughal governor shut himself in the castle. Shivaji raided Surat again in 1670.
steps.today: Today: Surat, Gujarat, India’s diamond-cutting city.

steps.title: A fort in the sea
steps.text: Shivaji saw that the Konkan needed a navy. He built warships and sea forts against the Siddis of Janjira, the Portuguese and the English. Sindhudurg, on an island off Malvan, was begun in 1664 and took about three years. Tradition says its walls hold Shivaji’s handprint and footprint, pressed in lime. In 1679 he fortified Khanderi island, despite English opposition.
steps.today: Today: Sindhudurg fort, off Malvan, Maharashtra, with a shrine to Shivaji inside.

steps.title: Purandar and Agra
steps.text: In 1665 the Rajput general Jai Singh besieged Purandar, and Shivaji agreed to give up 23 forts. He was persuaded to visit Aurangzeb at Agra, but at court in May 1666 he was placed among lesser nobles, protested and was put under guard. In August he escaped, by tradition hidden in baskets of sweets, and returned to the Deccan.
steps.today: Today: Agra Fort, Uttar Pradesh, a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Crowned at Raigad
steps.text: On 6 June 1674 Shivaji was crowned at Raigad by Gaga Bhatt, a scholar from Varanasi, taking the title Chhatrapati, lord of the royal parasol. The coronation made him a king in his own right, not a rebel against Bijapur or the Mughals. He ruled with a council of eight ministers (Ashtapradhan). Jijabai died days later.
steps.today: Today: Raigad fort, Maharashtra, where Shivaji’s samadhi stands.

steps.title: The southern campaign
steps.text: In 1677 Shivaji marched south in alliance with the sultan of Golconda, Abul Hasan Qutb Shah. He took Gingee and Vellore in the Tamil country and claimed his father’s lands from his half-brother Venkoji of Thanjavur. These southern forts mattered later, when the Mughals overran the Deccan. Shivaji died at Raigad in April 1680, aged about fifty.
steps.today: Today: Gingee fort, Villupuram district, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Sambhaji’s war
steps.text: Shivaji’s eldest son, Sambhaji, took the throne after a short struggle. In 1681 Aurangzeb came south with his court and armies, and stayed for the rest of his life. Sambhaji held him off for eight years while fighting the Siddis and Portuguese too. In 1689 he was captured at Sangameshwar, taken to Tulapur and executed after weeks of torture.
steps.today: Today: Vadhu Budruk, near Pune, where Sambhaji’s memorial stands; Sangameshwar is in Ratnagiri district.

steps.title: Rajaram at Gingee
steps.text: Raigad fell in 1689, and Sambhaji’s widow Yesubai and young son Shahu were taken prisoner. His brother Rajaram fled south in disguise to Gingee and ruled from there. Mughal armies besieged Gingee for about eight years. Meanwhile the commanders Santaji Ghorpade and Dhanaji Jadhav raided Mughal territory across the Deccan. Gingee fell in 1698, but Rajaram had already escaped.
steps.today: Today: Gingee, about 150 kilometres south-west of Chennai, Tamil Nadu.

steps.title: Tarabai’s war
steps.text: Rajaram died in 1700. His widow Tarabai, still in her twenties, took charge in the name of their young son, Shivaji II, and led the war herself. Aurangzeb, now over eighty, spent years besieging forts one by one; the Marathas often retook them once he moved on. Maratha raiders reached Malwa and Gujarat, and the war drained the Mughal treasury.
steps.today: Today: Panhala, a hill town inside the old fort walls, near Kolhapur, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Shahu returns
steps.text: Aurangzeb died at Ahmednagar in March 1707. The Mughals released Shahu, Sambhaji’s son, who had grown up in their camp, hoping he would divide the Marathas. He did: Tarabai called him an impostor, but many commanders joined him, and he won at Khed late in 1707. Shahu was crowned at Satara in 1708. A rival line later ruled from Kolhapur.
steps.today: Today: Satara, Maharashtra; Shahu’s descendants still live there, and Rajaram’s at Kolhapur.

steps.title: The admiral of the coast
steps.text: Kanhoji Angre commanded the Maratha fleet from his sea forts at Kolaba and Vijaydurg. He demanded passes from ships trading along the coast and seized those without them; the English, Dutch and Portuguese called him a pirate. Their attacks on his forts, including a joint English and Portuguese assault in 1721, failed. He died in 1729, still undefeated at sea.
steps.today: Today: Alibag, Raigad district, Maharashtra; the Navy’s base at Mumbai is INS Angre.

steps.title: The march to Delhi
steps.text: Shahu made Balaji Vishwanath his chief minister (Peshwa) in 1713. In 1718 and 1719 Balaji marched to Delhi with a Maratha army, allied with the Sayyid brothers, the kingmakers at the Mughal court. The emperor Farrukhsiyar was deposed, and the new court granted the Marathas a quarter (chauth) and a further tenth (sardeshmukhi) of the Deccan’s revenue.
steps.today: Today: the Red Fort, Old Delhi, a World Heritage Site.

steps.title: Baji Rao at Palkhed
steps.text: Balaji’s son Baji Rao became Peshwa in 1720, aged about twenty. The Nizam-ul-Mulk, who had made Hyderabad his own state, backed a rival Maratha claimant and invaded Maratha lands. Baji Rao refused open battle, raided the Nizam’s country and then trapped his army near Palkhed, cut off from water. The Nizam made peace and recognised Shahu’s claims.
steps.today: Today: Palkhed, Aurangabad district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Malwa and the gates of Delhi
steps.text: Baji Rao’s armies moved north into Malwa and Bundelkhand, where in 1729 he helped the Bundela ruler Chhatrasal against a Mughal general. In 1737 he raided up to the outskirts of Delhi. The Nizam came north to stop him and was surrounded near Bhopal. In the treaty that followed, early in 1738, Malwa was promised to the Marathas.
steps.today: Today: Bhopal, capital of Madhya Pradesh.

steps.title: The siege of Vasai
steps.text: Baji Rao’s brother Chimaji Appa turned on the Portuguese, who held the northern Konkan coast from their fortress at Bassein (Vasai). After a long campaign and a siege of about three months, with heavy losses on both sides, the fort surrendered in May 1739. The Portuguese kept Goa and Daman. Baji Rao died the next year, aged about forty.
steps.today: Today: Vasai fort, Palghar district, north of Mumbai.

steps.title: Raids into Bengal
steps.text: Raghuji Bhonsle, the Maratha ruler of Nagpur, sent cavalry into Bengal almost every year from 1741. The raiders, called bargis in Bengal, burned villages and drove many people from their homes; Bengali poems and lullabies still remember them. In 1751 the nawab Alivardi Khan made peace, ceding Orissa’s revenue and promising a yearly payment.
steps.today: Today: Murshidabad, West Bengal; Calcutta’s old Maratha Ditch was dug against the raiders.

steps.title: Flags beyond Attock
steps.text: Baji Rao’s son Balaji Bajirao, called Nanasaheb, became Peshwa in 1740. In 1757 the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani sacked Delhi. In 1758 an army under the Peshwa’s brother Raghunathrao drove the Afghans from Lahore and reached Attock on the Indus. The Marathi phrase ‘flags beyond Attock’ (Atkepar zende) still means a far-reaching triumph.
steps.today: Today: Attock fort, Punjab, Pakistan.

steps.title: The third battle of Panipat
steps.text: Ahmad Shah Durrani returned. A great Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau, the Peshwa’s cousin, marched north, but entrenched at Panipat for weeks, it ran short of food. On 14 January 1761 it attacked and was destroyed. Sadashivrao Bhau and the Peshwa’s heir, Vishwasrao, died. Deaths, including camp followers killed after the battle, are disputed estimates in the tens of thousands.
steps.today: Today: Panipat, Haryana, where the Kala Amb memorial marks the battlefield.

steps.title: Madhavrao’s recovery
steps.text: The Peshwa Nanasaheb died months after Panipat. His son Madhavrao, aged sixteen, restored Maratha power: he defeated the Nizam in 1763, fought Hyder Ali of Mysore and sent armies back to the north. He ruled from Shaniwar Wada, the Peshwas’ palace in Pune. He died of tuberculosis in 1772, aged twenty-seven; his brother Narayanrao was murdered there in 1773.
steps.today: Today: Shaniwar Wada, Pune; only its walls and gates survived a fire in 1828.

steps.title: Ahilyabai at Maheshwar
steps.text: The Holkars, Scindias, Gaekwads and Bhonsles became great houses of a Maratha confederacy, loyal to the Peshwa in name. Ahilyabai Holkar, widowed young, ruled the Holkar lands from Maheshwar on the Narmada for nearly thirty years. She was known for justice and fair taxes, and paid for temples, wells, rest houses and river steps (ghats) from Kashi to Somnath.
steps.today: Today: Maheshwar, Madhya Pradesh, still known for its ghats and Maheshwari saris.

steps.title: Mahadji Scindia in the north
steps.text: Mahadji Scindia survived Panipat and rebuilt Maratha power in the north. In 1771 he escorted the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II back to Delhi. He fought the British to a standstill, and the Treaty of Salbai in 1782 ended the first Anglo-Maratha War. From 1784 he ran the emperor’s government, with an army drilled by European officers.
steps.today: Today: Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh; the Scindias’ Jai Vilas Palace is partly a museum.

steps.title: The Treaty of Bassein
steps.text: Mahadji died in 1794 and Nana Phadnavis, the minister who had held the Peshwa’s court together, in 1800. The young Peshwa Baji Rao II quarrelled with the great houses. When Yashwantrao Holkar defeated him outside Pune in 1802, Baji Rao fled to the British, and at Bassein accepted a British force at Pune, paid for with his own lands.
steps.today: Today: Vasai, in Mumbai’s metropolitan region, Maharashtra.

steps.title: Assaye
steps.text: Daulatrao Scindia and Raghuji Bhonsle II refused to accept the treaty, and war followed. At Assaye, Arthur Wellesley, later Duke of Wellington, attacked a much larger Maratha army and won at heavy cost. Further north, Gerard Lake took Delhi and the emperor into British protection. By 1805 the British held Delhi, Agra, Orissa and Broach in Gujarat.
steps.today: Today: Assaye, a village in Jalna district, Maharashtra.

steps.title: The last Peshwa
steps.text: In November 1817 Baji Rao II turned on the British, burning their residency at Pune, but lost at Khadki. On 1 January 1818 a small Company force held Koregaon against his army. He surrendered in June and was exiled with a pension to Bithoor on the Ganga. The office of Peshwa ended; the British kept Shivaji’s descendants at Satara.
steps.today: Today: Bithoor, near Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh, home of Nana Sahib, who led the 1857 rising at Kanpur.

steps.title: Forts of a world heritage
steps.text: In July 2025 UNESCO listed twelve forts as the Maratha Military Landscapes of India: Salher, Shivneri, Lohagad, Khanderi, Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Suvarnadurg, Panhala, Vijaydurg and Sindhudurg in Maharashtra, and Gingee in Tamil Nadu. Shivaji’s memory is everywhere in Maharashtra, in statues, place names, Mumbai’s airport and railway terminus, and the festival of his birth, Shiv Jayanti.
steps.today: Today: Raigad, Maharashtra; Shiv Jayanti, 19 February, is a public holiday in the state.

items.name: Shivaji
items.role: Founder of the kingdom, Chhatrapati from 1674
items.text: Shivaji grew a few hill forts above Pune into a kingdom that held off both Bijapur and the Mughal empire. He used swift light cavalry, surprise raids, hill and sea forts, and a navy. He paid many officers in cash rather than land grants, to keep them loyal to the state. He is Maharashtra’s great hero.

items.name: Jijabai
items.text: Jijabai, daughter of the Maratha noble Lakhuji Jadhav of Sindkhed, raised Shivaji at Pune while her husband Shahaji served Bijapur in the south. Maratha tradition gives her a large part in shaping his sense of duty and his early government. She lived to see his coronation at Raigad in June 1674 and died days later.

items.name: Sambhaji
items.text: Shivaji’s eldest son went with him to Agra in 1666 and later wrote in Sanskrit. As Chhatrapati he fought the Mughals, the Siddis of Janjira and the Portuguese at once, and kept Aurangzeb’s huge armies busy for eight years. His capture and death in 1689 made him a martyr in Maratha memory, though earlier chroniclers judged him harshly.

items.name: Tarabai
items.role: Regent who led the war against Aurangzeb
items.text: Daughter of the general Hambirrao Mohite and wife of Rajaram, Tarabai led the Maratha war against Aurangzeb from 1700 in her son’s name; even the Mughal historian Khafi Khan praised her skill. After Shahu’s return she kept a rival court in the south until 1714. Late in life she fought the Peshwas for control at Satara, and died in 1761.

items.name: Baji Rao I
items.text: Peshwa at about twenty, Baji Rao led the Maratha armies north for twenty years and, by most accounts, never lost a battle. He relied on speed: light cavalry that lived off the land and outmarched slower Mughal armies. His love for Mastani, said to be a daughter of Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand, divided his family and is still retold.

items.name: Ahilyabai Holkar
items.role: Ruler of the Holkar lands, 1767 to 1795
items.text: Born in a village family, Ahilyabai married into the Holkars and lost her husband in battle in 1754. After her father-in-law Malharrao Holkar died in 1766, she took charge and ruled from Maheshwar until her death. She heard petitions herself, kept the Holkar lands largely at peace and is credited with founding Maheshwar’s weaving trade.

items.name: Mahadji Scindia
items.text: Lamed at Panipat, where he escaped the rout, Mahadji Scindia, from a family of the Peshwas’ commanders, became the strongest Maratha commander in the north. He hired the French officer Benoît de Boigne to train infantry and artillery on European lines. As the emperor’s regent from 1784 he controlled Delhi, and his house ruled Gwalior until 1947.

items.name: Nana Phadnavis
items.text: Nana Phadnavis survived Panipat and became the Peshwas’ chief minister. After Narayanrao’s murder in 1773 he and a council of ministers ruled for the infant Peshwa Sawai Madhavrao. He kept the Maratha houses together against the British, Mysore and the Nizam; his death in 1800 is often seen as the end of that unity.
